title: Parental Choice Is Sending Public Schools a Message. Are They Listening? ening/
author: Anna J. Egalite
summary: Anna Egalite argues that public school leaders should treat rising homeschooling rates not as a threat but as actionable feedback about what families want. Using North Carolina as a case study, she shows that public school dissatisfaction is now the leading reason parents cite for homeschooling, rising from 25.6% in 2020-21 to 51.5% in 2025-26. She proposes adding optional follow-up questions to homeschool registration forms so districts can precisely understand what families are seeking.
points: In 2025-26, 51.5% of NC parents cited public school dissatisfaction as their primary reason for homeschooling
Homeschool openings remain elevated post-pandemic; 12,643 new openings in 2025-26 vs 9,481 pre-pandemic
Public school dissatisfaction is now 12 times more common as a stated reason than private school dissatisfaction
Forward-thinking districts are treating school choice as information, not threat, and building new options in response
Egalite proposes optional follow-up questions on homeschool registration forms to capture precisely why families leave
quotes: West Virginia Board of Education President Paul Hardesty recently put the new reality plainly: Public schools are "competing for enrollment, whether we want to believe it or not.

policymakers should resist the temptation to explain the homeschool boom away as a pandemic artifact, a lifestyle preference, or a purely ideological choice. In North Carolina, many parents are saying something much more direct: The public school system is not the best place for my child.
If we're going to be the first choice for families, then we need to understand why some families are choosing not to send their kids to us.

The best public school leaders are not hiding from school choice; they're learning from it. They are building new public options, highlighting pathways families may not know about, and creating better channels for parent voice.

If families are saying that the public school system does not work for them, system leaders should seize the opportunity to ask why, study the answers, and use what they learn to become more accommodating, more receptive, and more accessible to the families they hope to serve.
